title: Chapter 1: Today is a Good Day to Throw My Life Away 4
content: It was the most luxurious room in the most extravagant inn in the town.
Of course, it was only fitting for Erika Solnzali, the daughter of a marquis family and the Prime Minister's daughter, to stay here. There was no doubt about that.
But why was I sharing a room with her?

After entering the town and asking a craftsman to repair the carriage, I wrote a letter to report the attack on the Prime Minister and requested the Adventurer Guild to ensure it was delivered safely.
While I was at it, I replenished my supply of daggers after smashing the head of the attacker who had flown off somewhere, and by the time I finished, it was just the right time for dinner.

During that time, while Erika Solnzali didn’t act overly excited, she seemed to be enjoying herself throughout the meal, eating even the cheap dishes that were worlds apart from what she usually consumed with an appetite.
By the way, for me, those dishes were not just ordinary; they were even more expensive than what I typically ate.

After dinner, just as we were about to head to the inn, Merseja said he would sleep in the carriage since he needed to keep an eye on it. He handed me the bag containing our change of clothes and went off to the stables attached to the inn.
Well, he was both the coachman and a bodyguard, so I figured that was part of his job. I went with Erika Solnzali to the inn's reception, where we were handed a single room key.
The receptionist seemed puzzled when she saw my face, and a man who looked like the manager noticed it. I hoped he would forgive her.
I was aware that I had a rather intense expression.
Why was there only one room prepared for us?
The answer was quite simple. We were in the middle of a farce.
In other words, if someone were to follow our tracks later, it would be strange for two people, whose heads had boiled over from eloping, to stay in separate rooms.
One might wonder who would investigate such a thing, but the most likely candidate would be the Lady Light Priestess. If she had any doubts about this farce, she would surely look into it.
After all, she knew Erika Solnzali very well.
So it wouldn’t be strange for her to feel suspicious about this charade.
Of course, the Light Priestess wouldn’t investigate directly.
It wasn’t a matter of ability; rather, those around her wouldn’t allow it.
Convincing the Light Priestess not to be displeased would be a challenge, but they would manage somehow. They might say something about not disturbing the blessings of the two or some such.
That was the purpose of this farce.
So what would the Light Priestess do? Most likely, she would commission the Adventurer Guild.
In this case, one might question whether a mere commoner and student like her could afford the commission fee, but that was not an issue. The guild wouldn’t charge her.
In fact, just the fact that it was a request from the Light Priestess could lead to a swarm of adventurers taking it on for free, even if the task was something as mundane as cleaning a ditch.
Being the Light Priestess was truly no trivial matter.
If adventurers were involved, it would become difficult for the kingdom to exert influence.
In other words, it would be hard to cover up.
Thus, we had to create the fact that we stayed in the same room.
A letter from the Prime Minister explaining such reasons was left in the room.
In the last line, it was written in trembling letters, “I trust you, Shin Longdagger-kun.”
I quietly averted my eyes from the strong emotions conveyed through the writing.

If he was going to write that much, he should have just colluded with the inn to make it look like we stayed in the same room. But I supposed he thought that if he tried to manipulate every inn until we left the country, it would become too large-scale and more likely to be discovered.
Even with trembling letters, the Prime Minister remained calm.
“Father can be foolish sometimes, can’t he? He misjudges your resolve, Shin Longdagger.”
Those were the words of Erika Solnzali after finishing reading the letter.
What did he mean by my resolve? I was in a state of utter confusion, suddenly finding myself sharing a room with Erika Solnzali.
“This is nothing short of an insult. I shall apologize on behalf of my father, Shin Longdagger.”
Erika Solnzali’s sincere apology only deepened my confusion, but I shook my head to convey that no apology was necessary.
Seeing me, Erika Solnzali smiled and said, “You’re right; an apology itself would be rude.”
What is this?
As expected of the most luxurious inn in the town, there was even a separate bath for men and women.
Moreover, to my surprise, the bath was filled with hot water.
Perhaps because I usually relied on purification magic or due to my usual frugality, I found myself feeling anxious about dirtying the water while soaking in the bath.
…Just kidding.
Rather than feeling anxious, my mind was filled with the reality that I had to spend the night in the same room as Erika Solnzali.
What should I do?

Should I talk about something to keep her entertained? I’m not bragging, but I have absolutely no stock of topics that would please a girl. I’ve heard that talking about flowers and plants can be well-received, but should I discuss medicinal herbs that have calming effects?
No, that’s impossible. I have no confidence in making a conversation about herbs last through the night. Should I mix in some talk about the shapes of trees that can be used for traps?
No, that wouldn’t work, I scolded myself.

I’m not bragging, but in the three years since I entered the academy at thirteen, I’ve never had any luck with girls, and I haven’t even managed to make a “normal” female friend, so it’s fundamentally impossible.
I was aware that I was thinking about pointless things to divert my eyes from reality, but I also had a strong conviction that I wouldn’t be able to look her in the face otherwise.

Maybe that’s why, as I pondered whether it would be okay to talk about seasonal medicinal herbs, the moment I opened the door to the room, I was struck speechless, my thoughts thrown aside by the sight before me.
She was simply beautiful.
Erika Solnzali was beautiful.
In the nightgown provided by the inn, her damp hair from the bath was exposed to the night air on the balcony, and the sight was nothing short of beautiful.
Though I couldn’t see her face from behind, I could tell she was relaxed, enveloped in a golden aura of magic.
I found myself standing next to her as if drawn in.
Since I couldn’t see her directly at the academy, I had always tried to stay close enough to catch a glimpse of her profile.
Compared to those days, the distance between us was much closer now.
So I realized that she wasn’t relaxed at all.
She was gazing into the dimly lit town, lost in thought.
Suddenly, I wanted to know what Erika Solnzali was thinking.
Was it about the academy?
About her family she had parted from?
About those who had exiled her?
Or perhaps about her best friend, the Light Priestess?
Whatever it was, I wanted to listen to her and respond.
[img]https://i.imgur.com/NKFuZTF.jpeg
Whether it was worries, complaints, anxieties about the future, or hopes and desires for what lay ahead.
I wanted to hear her story and respond.
I wanted to tell her that I was there for her.
“Shin Longdagger.”
Suddenly, she called my name, and I remembered how to breathe.
I could say I returned to my senses.
My heart raced, and I felt a sudden tightness in my chest.
This was bad; I suppressed the instinct to keep looking at her profile and shifted my gaze to the town.
I focused on the cobblestone streets illuminated by the scattered streetlights to calm my heart.
Since our room was on the fourth floor, I could see the quiet town quite well.
Counting the cobblestones, I recalled what a senior adventurer once told me: counting helps calm a person.
From beside me, I sensed a hesitant voice and a faint gaze directed at me.
“Is this your first time too?”
What do you mean?!
Someone, anyone, please praise me for not shouting, for not flinching, and for being able to respond calmly without stumbling over my words.
I said, no, I was able to say.
“What do you mean?”
In my mind, I was screaming, “W-What do you mean?!”
Erika Solnzali let out a hesitant sigh and said to me.
Please stop, that sigh is too much; my heart can’t take it.
“I mean killing someone.”
She began speaking without waiting for my response.
“It was my first time.”
Yet there was no sense of regret in her voice.
If there was anything, it was perhaps confusion?
“However, I don’t feel it. I thought of that as a monster.”
By the way, monsters and the Demon Race are different entities.
Many who have never seen a Demon Race might confuse the two, but anyone who has seen them will undoubtedly say they are different.
When facing a monster, one does not feel the intense aversion one feels towards the Demon Race.
The Demon Race is a mysterious existence that appears suddenly, wreaks havoc, and is subjugated, clearly distinct from monsters.
The church calls them the unblessed, and adventurers say they are a nuisance that yields nothing when defeated.
Since they are not encountered as frequently as monsters, I have only fought a few times, and even among seasoned adventurers, it’s not uncommon for someone to have never encountered one.
Naturally, Erika Solnzali, being a marquis daughter, had likely never faced a monster. In the academy, practical combat is a task assigned in the fourth year.
Her experience of taking a life would have been limited to killing livestock with her own sword during academy assignments.
“Even now that you’ve told me that it was once a human, to be honest, I still don’t feel it.”
Erika Solnzali lightly shook her head.
“I’m not doubting you or anything. It just feels somewhat rude to not feel anything after having killed.”
Saying this, she searched for coherent words, her gaze wandering in the air.
Seeing her profile, words naturally came to me.
“I was also a first-timer, Erika Solnzali.”
I looked up at the night sky and closed my eyes.
I pictured the faces of the men I had killed today. They were all ordinary men, the kind you could find anywhere.
They didn’t have particularly bad looks; they were just common men, just like those in this town.
“But I have no regrets.”
I could assert that and mean it.
“I could protect you; I decided for myself that I would protect you.”
If one is a noble, let me declare this.
Whether one is aware of it or not, someday, someone will die by their own decision.
It may be when they order the execution of a criminal or when they sacrifice a few for the benefit of many.
But that moment will inevitably come.
As the second son who wouldn’t inherit the family, the likelihood of me making such decisions directly was low.
However, when the family decides, it means that I, as part of that family, also bear the weight of that decision and its consequences.
But I was not a first-timer who could even question that awareness.
I had decided, of my own will, to protect Erika Solnzali, to want to protect her.
There was no regret in that.
Even recalling the faces of the men I had killed today, I did not regret my first time.
It might just be a selfish thought, but I didn’t want her to feel ambiguous about it either.
“What were you thinking when you swung your sword back then?”
I asked her, and her wandering gaze captured mine.
Erika Solnzali thought for a moment and then smiled, a smile that resembled a wry grin.
“I thought I had to protect the coachman… and my tired bodyguard.”
To be precise, it was the coachman and my husband, she added with a laugh.
“In that case,”
I said, to convey that your decision and its outcome were not products of ambiguity.
“I should thank you. Erika Solnzali, thank you for wielding your sword for my sake.”
A brief silence followed by a small nod.
After that, she responded, “You’re welcome,” and turned her body toward me.
“In that case, I too would like to express my gratitude, Shin Longdagger. Your sword cleared the dew that stood in my path.”
Even now—she added with a smile.
“Speaking of which,”
Erika Solnzali said as if she had recalled something, and just as we both returned our gazes to the town, she continued.
“Shin Longdagger, calling me by my full name is a declaration of your resolve, and I took that to heart, but… it’s rather troublesome.”
I realized that she had misunderstood something.
I didn’t know what kind of resolve it was to call her Erika Solnzali, but that had nothing to do with it.
It was simply that I was too embarrassed to call her Erika.
No, it’s impossible to call her by her name.
“I will call you Shin from now on. You should call me Erika.”
Isn’t that a high difficulty?
Before I could even clear up the misunderstanding, the difficulty level shot up, and I felt a chill run down my spine.
“This isn’t to disregard your resolve or feelings; it’s just for the next year—”
“Erika.”
I said it impulsively.
I had said it.
An awkward silence fell over the balcony.
After telling me to call her, she fell silent when I did; couldn’t she spare me from that? I felt like I was going to die from embarrassment.
“Yes, let’s go with that, Shin.”
She broke the silence with a laugh, Erika Solnzali, Erika, shimmering with golden magic.
“Besides, I was mistaken.”
Erika teased with a smile.
“I am no longer a Solnzali; I am now a Longdagger. If we’re to be correct, it should be Erika Longdagger, my husband.”
With that, she left the balcony.
That was close…
I almost jumped off the balcony.
That night.
Every time I recalled her calling me “husband” while lying in bed, I felt like I was going to thrash around in the sheets.
So she had quite a bad sleeping posture, huh?
I did it.
I really did it.
Erika Solnzali recalled her words and actions in bed, feeling a wave of regret wash over her, and she wanted nothing more than to bury her head in her hands and roll around.
What was this “Erika Longdagger” nonsense? Was my head boiling over? As she remembered her own words, she squirmed in embarrassment, thrashing about in the bed.
It was completely impulsive, pure 100% impulse.
I can’t help it, Erika thought, covering her mouth to stifle the scream that threatened to escape due to her embarrassment.
That was unacceptable, truly unacceptable.
Even she understood, as her best friend would say, that her clumsy maiden circuits were malfunctioning.
That was Shin’s sincere words of comfort. Thank you for killing for me, whether that could truly be considered comforting or not. It was an expression of his kindness.
She felt that, as a proper noble daughter, she was quite lacking.
Could there be such a foolish story? A person who had been thoroughly educated on the mindset and resolve expected of a noble daughter, someone who had already made up her mind long ago.
To feel so relieved just from a single phrase like “Thank you for killing for me,” was there really such a ridiculous story?
No, in truth, she felt relieved, and to put it plainly, she was aware that she had been saved.
She was, indeed.
Erika covered her face with her hands and squirmed.
Is it really okay? To feel relieved and saved by “I killed for you, thank you for killing for me,” and then to be so giddy about it, and what’s this about calling him “husband”?
Words came out of her mouth that made her feel as if flowers were blooming in her head, words that shouldn’t have come out.
Erika thrashed about in bed again. It was unladylike, but she couldn’t help it.

What a strange boy. Shin Longdagger was a strange boy. He spoke naturally even with someone like her, who felt particularly tense around both genders, and just when she thought he had a relaxed expression, he would suddenly reveal a glimpse of the strength beneath.
In that regard, he reminded her of her best friend, the Light Priestess.
Behind his seemingly carefree words lay a fierce resolve. He would abandon his life as a noble to think of a single woman. Did she like that purity about him?
Was it because he had treated her kindly, no matter how he comforted her, that she had become so giddy? She recalled her earlier self and thrashed about again.
Erika took a moment to calm her breathing and think.

Shin, sleeping in the next bed, was quiet; had he already fallen asleep? For a moment, she thought it was unfair, but to him, a series of words was just an act of kindness, an expression of his gentleness.
She took a deep breath and exhaled.
He was the kind of person who would throw his life away just to gain acquaintance with the Light Priestess and take on the role of a farcical husband.
If that were the case, he would surely be kind to her, the wife role he had to fulfill. That should be the case, Erika thought.
In other words, it was Shin’s fault.
Erika concluded this, and it was just a figment of her imagination that her heart was racing a little.
And it was Shin who made her heart race.
His resolve was good, but he might be a bit of an enemy to maidens.
With such thoughts swirling in her mind, Erika drifted off to sleep.
